newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: EXPORTS SEEN HELPING AILING SAFRICA TEXTILE SECTOR.
newsitem.headline: EXPORTS SEEN HELPING AILING SAFRICA TEXTILE SECTOR.

text.p: South Africa's embattled textile sector may in future find some respite in growing export opportunities as world tariffs are cut and foreign capital flows into local firms, a credit risk insurer said on Tuesday.
John Thornton, senior manager of Credit Guarantee Insurance Corp of Africa Ltd, said that the textile industry, which has been hardhit by years of illegal imports, was in better shape than expected.
"The American Congress is looking at dispensing with duties on U.S. imports from Sub-Saharan Africa. This will almost certainly lead to factories being set up," Thornton said in a statement.
"(Textile manufacturers) ability to manufacture world-class items, particularly in smaller runs, will stand them in good stead in the expanding export market," he said.
He said that Indonesians, who had been investing in South African textile businesses, had found the move "tough" but that they looked to becoming big players.

A study by South Africa's Industrial Development Corp recently found that the country's footwear manufacturers would also have to sharpen their focus on exports in the medium to upper segments of the market in a bid to lift the stranglehold of cheap imports.
But Luke Doig, Credit Gurantee senior manager for economic and investment services said that this industry faced an uphill battle following the flood of imports which have buffetted local production.

"We are particularly concerned about import penetration in South Africa standing at a crippling 60 percent. The unacceptability becomes apparent when compared to other middle income regions like Taiwan (16 percent), South Korea (seven percent) and South America (one percent)," Doig said.
He said that footwear imports had grown from 17 million pairs of shoes in 1991 to 55 million pairs in 1996. Domestic production had falled from 72.6 millin pairs in 1992 to 46.8 million last year.

The smuggling of clothes, mainly from the East, had also led to a significant reduction in manufacturing as several operations relocated to Malawi and Mozambique, where lower costs allow better competition with international producers.
